doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: Outlook for new jazz graduates and the New York scene
summary: He discusses saturated teaching jobs, New York's varied work versus Los Angeles, and his advice to students.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: I would think so, yeah. Well just to wrap up here, every year there’s thousands of graduates of jazz schools coming into the market. What’s your outlook for them?

Depends where you go I guess. It seems — I think in another ten years we’re going to really find out what happens with all this. Because for the past 15 years all these jazz programs have been supplying new teachers for the jazz programs. So you’ve got a lot of really, really good teachers in jazz programs now. Much more accomplished than the old days. You’ve got a lot of great jazz programs everywhere. But then the question is where does everybody else go now that all these jobs are filled. There’s no more road bands so the answer is a lot of people are getting into one of the military bands or doing cruise ship work, things like that. You can’t even move to a place like Las Vegas anymore and make a living very well. So it’s a very different thing. New York is probably one of the few places where anybody that’s got anything together can move to New York and eke out a living, because there’s so many different things going on. You’ve got Broadway, you’ve got live work, you’ve got a club date scene which is playing weddings and things like that. In New York it’s like beyond professional level. You know, these giant weddings and they play with these 10-piece groups that are slick and polished with giant sound systems and all that stuff. That’s a big, big industry in New York. And there’s just a lot of live venues and live gigs and there’s orchestras and symphonies and the opera and all that stuff. There’s plenty of little places where guys can kind of combine all this stuff to make a living doing this and that and this and that. Los Angeles I think is a little more smaller scope. It’s got the studio scene and a little bit of live work that maybe tours, but it’s mostly commercial music for the most part and not a lot of jazz clubs out there. So it’s kind of not as multi-faceted as New York. So we’ll see, we’ll see. But I think, I tell students all the time, I mean what do you say to these students that want to be musicians? I say well if they’re like me there’s no choice. I had to be a musician. There was nothing else I wanted to do. I would have been miserable being anything else. So you’ve got to take your shot. And if you apply yourself and do all the right things you’re going to make a success of yourself. And if you don’t then it’s on you. And so I think there’s still room for people. The Broadway scene in New York is very healthy right now. There’s a lot of musicians making really good livings.
